lesson.title: Dividing Functions Without Dividing Their Derivatives
lesson.summary: The quotient rule is derived directly from the product rule by treating the numerator as the quotient times the denominator, revealing why the formula has a subtraction and a squared denominator.
lesson.body:
Just as multiplying two functions does not let you simply multiply their derivatives, dividing two functions does not let you simply divide them either. Rather than starting the quotient rule from scratch with the limit definition, it is faster and more illuminating to lean on the product rule you just derived. Suppose q(x) = f(x) / g(x), where g(x) is never 0. Multiplying both sides by g(x) gives the equivalent statement f(x) = q(x) g(x), an equation between two functions that are equal everywhere, and equal functions have equal derivatives.

Differentiate both sides of f(x) = q(x)g(x) using the product rule on the right side. The left side differentiates to f'(x), and the right side, treating q(x) and g(x) as the two factors, differentiates to q'(x)g(x) + q(x)g'(x). This gives the equation f'(x) = q'(x)g(x) + q(x)g'(x). The unknown here is q'(x), so isolate it: q'(x)g(x) = f'(x) - q(x)g'(x), and then q'(x) = [f'(x) - q(x)g'(x)] / g(x).

This is correct but still has q(x) sitting inside its own derivative formula, so substitute q(x) = f(x)/g(x) back in: q'(x) = [f'(x) - (f(x)/g(x)) g'(x)] / g(x). Multiplying numerator and denominator by g(x) to clear the inner fraction gives q'(x) = [f'(x)g(x) - f(x)g'(x)] / [g(x)]^2. This is the quotient rule: the derivative of f(x)/g(x) equals f'(x)g(x) minus f(x)g'(x), all over g(x) squared. The subtraction, unlike the addition in the product rule, is essential, and so is squaring the denominator, both features falling directly out of solving the product rule equation rather than being arbitrary additions.

A worked example ties this together. Let q(x) = (x^2 + 1)/(x - 1), so f(x) = x^2+1 with f'(x) = 2x, and g(x) = x-1 with g'(x) = 1. The quotient rule gives q'(x) = [2x(x-1) - (x^2+1)(1)] / (x-1)^2 = [2x^2 - 2x - x^2 - 1] / (x-1)^2 = (x^2 - 2x - 1)/(x-1)^2. At x = 2, this evaluates to (4 - 4 - 1)/(2-1)^2 = -1/1 = -1.

A quick numerical check confirms the sign and rough size of that answer. q(2) = (4+1)/(2-1) = 5, and q(2.01) = (4.0401+1)/1.01 = 5.0401/1.01, which is approximately 4.9902. The difference quotient [4.9902 - 5]/0.01 is about -0.98, close to the exact value of -1 found from the formula, with the small gap simply coming from using a finite step size of 0.01 instead of a true limit. The negative slope also makes sense visually, since near x = 2 this rational function is decreasing.

A useful sanity check on the formula itself is to specialize it to a case you already fully understand: let g(x) be a nonzero constant c. Then q(x) = f(x)/c, and the quotient rule gives q'(x) = [f'(x)c - f(x)*0]/c^2 = c f'(x)/c^2 = f'(x)/c, exactly matching the constant multiple rule from the basic derivative rules, which says dividing a function by a constant simply divides its derivative by that same constant. This kind of check, reducing a new formula to a simpler known case, is a good habit whenever a rule feels complicated. It is also worth remembering where q(x) and its derivative are even defined: both the original function and the quotient rule formula require g(x) to be nonzero, and at any x where g(x) = 0 neither the function nor its derivative exists, no matter how well behaved f and g are individually, so keeping track of these excluded points is part of correctly stating the domain of q'(x), not an afterthought to skip.
